data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a pragmatic, non-inductive rule of action based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness), where the cost is accepting that we can never know if our theories are true, only that they are closer to the truth than their falsified rivals.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the logical incoherence of Popper's formal definition of verisimilitude (as shown by Tich\u00fd and Miller) renders the concept unusable for comparing false theories.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory necessarily implies an inductive belief in its future success, regardless of the stated intent.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper replaces the inductive goal of 'probability' with the comparative goal of 'verisimilitude'. A theory that survives severe tests has demonstrated higher content and resilience, suggesting it captures more truth-content and less falsity-content than a refuted rival. The preference is rational not because the theory is likely true, but because it is the best available approximation of truth we have, making it the only rational basis for action.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
